Claude Fable 5.2 is #1 on four independent leaderboards one day after launch: 65 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, 71.31% on the Vals Index, 174 on Epoch's Capabilities Index and 84.9 on LiveBench. On the same Artificial Analysis board at max effort it ranks 73rd of 73 on cost per task and 72nd of 73 on speed. Both facts are true, and the second one decides most of what this model is good for.
Anthropic released Fable 5.2 on November 9, 2026, alongside Claude Mythos 5.2. I went through the launch post, docs, pricing page, third-party leaderboards, long-form reviews, the Hacker News thread and X reactions. Below is what I could verify, by category, with a tier list and a list of what I could not confirm.
🧭 "Vendor" means Anthropic's own published number. "Independent" means a third party ran it and published it on its own site.
What Fable 5.2 actually is 🧠
Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are the same underlying model. Fable ships with classifiers that block high-risk cybersecurity work (pen testing, exploit generation, binary vulnerability work) and most research-biology tasks. Mythos is the same weights with those safeguards relaxed, available only to vetted organizations through Anthropic's Cyber and Life Sciences Verification Programs.
Blocked requests get answered by an older model: Opus 4.8 for cyber, Opus 5 for biology. Anthropic also says it deliberately limited gains in accelerator kernel optimization and LLM architecture research during training, so in those areas Fable 5.2 performs at about Opus 5.5 level.
Anthropic's own positioning is modest. Its docs say to start with Opus 5.5 for most workloads and move to Fable 5.2 "for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work, or when your evals on Claude Opus 5.5 at higher effort still fall short." Fable can also run as an Advisor (a cheaper model consults it) or an Orchestrator (it delegates to smaller models).
Headline demos from the launch post, all vendor-reported:
🔧 Agents on an earlier Fable 5.2 build migrated a production service from Python to Rust; it now starts about 26x faster.
💻 One engineer had it coordinate 1,000+ subagents for eight days to build a prototype OS that boots on a laptop.
📐 About 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents formalized Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean in 30 hours. Opus 5.5 in the same setup completed 26% in 18 hours. The system card says this used an earlier snapshot.
🔌 From a one-paragraph prompt it designed three working electronic devices with four-layer boards, enclosures and firmware. All three worked without electrical changes.
⚛️ It is credited with solving two open problems about black holes. An independent read of the linked preprints found they attribute the work to an internal Claude research model prompted and checked by a physicist, with no peer review mentioned, and that Opus 5.5 later reached the second result on its own.
Treat these as capability demonstrations, not benchmarks. None has been rerun by an outside party.
Specs, availability and pricing 💵
📋 Fable 5.2 spec sheet
API model ID     claude-fable-5-2
Released         Nov 9, 2026
Context window   1M tokens, flat price at any length
Max output       128K tokens
Knowledge cutoff June 2026
Thinking         Adaptive, always on (cannot disable)
Effort levels    Low · Medium · High · Xhigh · Max
Default effort   High on API · Medium in apps and Claude Code
Input            Text, images, files (no video)
Platforms        Claude API, Bedrock, Google Cloud, MS Foundry
Retirement       Not sooner than Nov 9, 2027
💰 API price per 1M tokens
              Input   Output  Cache read  Batch in/out
Fable 5.2     $8      $40     $0.20       $4 / $20
Fable 5.2 ⚡   $16     $80     stacks      n/a
Fable 5.1     $10     $50     $0.25       $5 / $25
Opus 5.5      $4      $20     $0.20       $2 / $10
Sonnet 5.5    $2      $10     $0.10       $1 / $5
Three details matter more than the headline. The price fell 20% from Fable 5.1 on every line. Cache reads cost 2.5% of input on Fable 5.2, so Fable and Opus 5.5 both read cache at $0.20 per million, which narrows the gap for agent loops that resend big contexts. Fast mode (up to 2.5x faster generation) doubles the price and cannot be combined with Batch.
Not on the price sheet: both 5.2 models require 30-day data retention unless an organization is approved for zero data retention via a private beta called Enterprise Frontier Safeguards. One independent write-up of the rate-limit docs found the Start tier gives Fable a quarter of Opus 5.5's per-minute token allowance.
Developers migrating from Fable 5.1 should know about four breaking changes in Anthropic's migration notes: editing earlier turns now invalidates thinking blocks on every account, only 5.2 models can read 5.2 thinking, the older computer-use tool returns errors outside Bedrock, and the advisor tool needs a Fable 5.2 advisor.
For subscribers, the launch offer runs through November 16, 2026 at 11:59 pm PT. Pro and standard Team seats get Fable inside their plan for up to 50% of weekly limits plus one Fable reset. Max, Ultra and premium Team seats get one to three resets based on tenure, expiring March 8, 2027. Free is excluded, and paid billing had to be in place before November 9 at 10:00 am PT.

Two notes on the table. The Gemini column is Gemini 4 Carbon, which is still in limited release, while the system card's FrontierSWE section and the RoboDojo chart use Gemini 4 Argon. And the Mythos-only rows (CyScenarioBench 76.3%, CVE Rediscovery 89.6%, protein binder design 85.1%) are not things Fable users can access.
By VentureBeat's count, one of the two new models leads 13 of 15 score lines. The exceptions are AutomationBench (Gemini 4 Carbon) and AA-Briefcase head-to-head Elo, where Opus 5.5 scores 1,800 to Fable's 1,785 even though Fable passes more of the rubric (66.1% vs 61.2%).

On Vals, Sonnet 5.5, Gemini 4 Carbon and Opus 5.5 all sit near Fable's ±0.96 error band, and Sonnet costs a quarter of Fable's list price. On Artificial Analysis the lead is 5 points at max and 2 points at High.
Coding 👨‍💻
Coding has the clearest lead and the broadest evidence.
Vendor: 49.1% on FrontierCode 2.0 at Xhigh (run by Cognition), 69.9% on FrontierSWE v2 (run by Proximal). Two write-ups quoting the system card report 93.0% on SWE-bench Pro vs 89.9% for Opus 5.5, and 67.6% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 vs 66.4% for Opus 5.5, a gap smaller than the 1.8-point standard error.
Independent (Vals): #1 of 127 on Vibe Code Bench at 93.77%, #1 on Terminal-Bench 4.0 at 65.15% (tied with Opus 5.5), #1 of 66 on ProgramBench at 19.00% (Opus 18.50%), #2 on Code Migration at 83.27%. The weak row is SWE-bench Multimodal: 62.29% vs 70.21% for Opus 5.5.
The effort curve is the most useful finding. FrontierCode 2.0 per the system card, as reported by VentureBeat:
⚙️ FrontierCode 2.0: score vs $/task
Medium   37.6%  $2.48  ██
High     45.3%  $6.72  █████
Xhigh    49.1%  $14.19 ██████████
Max      45.7%  $44.70 ██████████████████████████████
Opus 5.5 Max  45.5%  $12.82
Astra Max     42.8%  $6.68
Max scored lower than Xhigh at about three times the cost. High matched Opus 5.5's best for about half the cost per task. Cursor's numbers in the system card show the same curve: 56.9% at High on about 99K output tokens per task, 60.0% at Max on about 353K.
Upgrading from Fable 5.1 can cut or raise your bill depending on the setting. Fable 5.2 at Medium beat Fable 5.1's best FrontierCode score by 5.2 points at about 71% lower cost per task. Pinned at Xhigh, it scored 16.7 points higher and cost about 63% more per task than 5.1 at Xhigh, despite the lower token price.
Developers landed in the same place. One X post summed it up as "Fable 5.2 High = Opus 5.5 Max, Fable 5.2 xHigh > any model, don't use Fable 5.2 Max." One Hacker News commenter said it was "burning through my task list." Others said they struggle to tell it apart from Opus 5.5 on ordinary coding.
Reasoning and math 🧮
Vendor: 74.2% on Humanity's Last Exam with tools vs 67.7% for Opus 5.5 and 57.2% for GPT-6 Astra. Anthropic says Low effort matches Opus 5.5's best HLE score for under a tenth of the cost.
Independent (Epoch): 95% on FrontierMath Tiers 1-3 and 100% on Tier 4, the best listed on both. GPQA Diamond is 94%, where GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Argon score 96%. SimpleQA Verified is 94% vs 72% for Opus 5.5. ARC Prize verified 93.8% on ARC-AGI-2.
One small independent test: six script-checked hard problems, three runs each at Low, Medium and High, no tools. Fable 5.2 got 52 of 54. A counting problem Fable 5.1 never solved after 17 to 22 minutes per try, 5.2 solved every time, usually in 3 to 7 minutes. Low got all 18 right for $1.22 per set.
Agents, computer use and knowledge work 🤖
The biggest gap in the release. On the Remote Labor Index, run by Scale AI on real paid freelance projects, Fable 5.2 scores 41.3% at High vs 21.3% for Opus 5.5 and 20.8% for GPT-6 Astra. Nothing else in the table doubles the next model.
OSWorld 2.1 partial is 89.3% vs 87.2% for Opus. On the strict version, VentureBeat reports 54.6% vs 53.2%. On Perplexity's WANDR data-collection test it scores 82.1% vs 72.3%.
Business workflows are weaker. AutomationBench rises from 39.7% at Low to 51.4% at Max, and Gemini 4 Carbon still leads at 53.9%. About half the cases still fail.
Domain work is mixed. Vals has it #1 on Finance Agent (69.47%) and BioMysteryBench (83.70%), but #20 of 37 on legal and #27 of 84 on tax. A financial-modeling startup reported 91% vs 86% for Fable 5.1. An accounting company reported a regression on its 101-task benchmark: 81.2% vs 85.1% for Fable 5.1, with accounts receivable at 33.3%. Per one tester quoting the system card, Opus 5.5 leads PhysicianBench 68.4% to 64.4%.
Writing ✍️
No independent writing score exists yet. Fable 5.2 is not on EQ-Bench Creative Writing or the LMArena text boards. For context, Fable 5.1 is third on EQ-Bench Creative Writing v3 at 2,155.3, behind GPT-6 Astra (2,176.9) and Kimi K3.1 Pro (2,172.6).
Anthropic claims 5.2 communicates "more clearly." The most detailed review I found, from a business-school professor with pre-release access, praises the range and then lists failure modes:
📝 A research paper that grew to 182 pages because "every critique got a new analysis and nothing was ever cut."
📝 Recurring "Claudespeak" inserted during revisions.
📝 A course site that was "accurate and joyless" on the first pass.
📝 A rule book for its own agent teams that reached 204 sections and 87,500 words.
The reviewer's line: its critic agents found errors, but none "asked whether the work was too long, too repetitive, or no fun." Artificial Analysis independently ranks Fable 5.2 (max) 72nd of 73 on verbosity. On Hacker News, opinions on Claude's prose split hard, with some calling Opus 5.5 the most readable model they use.
My read: strong on structure and accuracy, weak at knowing when to stop. Give it a length budget and a separate cut pass.
Design, frontend and vision 🎨
🎨 Design signals
AA-3D (Artificial Analysis, Elo)
 Fable 5.2   ████████████████████ 1271 ±25
 Sonnet 5.5  ██████████████████▉  1204
 Opus 5.5    ██████████████████▉  1202
 GPT-6 Astra ██████████████████▍  1168
 Gemini 4 Ar ██████████████████   1147
 Fable 5.1   █████████████████▉   1139

WebDev Arena  1832 ±18 (AutoEval, 0 votes)
LiveBench     Design category #1
DesignArena   not listed yet
The WebDev Arena figure is an automated estimate with no human votes, so it is a projection. AA-3D is a real run, and the 132-point jump over Fable 5.1 is large. One widely liked X post called it "another step up in visual design and polish." The professor's review found the taste gap here too: a first "beautiful" redesign came out as a kiddie bell-ringing game.
Vision is solid, not dominant. Chartography is 73.4%, 0.9 points over Gemini 4 Carbon. An independent object-detection board ranked it #1 of 44 on mAP 50-95 (0.347 vs 0.345 for GPT-6.1 Terra), at $37.55 per 1,000 images, but median time per image rose from 2.6 s to 4.6 s vs Fable 5.1 and refusals on an X-ray dataset rose from 1 to 10.
Long context 📚
1M tokens, no surcharge. One independent tester asked three questions about a server log at 150K and 892K tokens. All 10 answers were right, and caching the 892K document cost $8.93 vs $11.18 on Fable 5.1. One answer took two minutes where Opus 5.5 took six seconds. Per that tester, the system card's full-context ProgramBench has Opus 5.5 ahead, 91.2% to 85.6%.
Speed and latency ⏱️
Anthropic claims output up to 30% faster than Fable 5.1. Independent measurement, thinking included:
⏱️ Artificial Analysis, Fable 5.2 (max)
Output speed         103 tok/s
First answer token   231.55 s
Time per index task  44.1 min (median 12.9)
Speed rank           72nd of 73
Output tokens        275M (median 72.8M)
At low effort it is usable. One tester measured 4 to 4.5 s median per everyday answer, first token at 2.3 s on Low and 3.8 s on High, slower than Fable 5.1's sub-second starts. A Hacker News commenter called it "faster than I expected" on a big review.
Safety and alignment 🛡️
Anthropic rates high-stakes misalignment risk as low. Tests ran on Mythos 5.2. Positives: lower rates of hallucinated inputs and false claims of completion than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Mythos 5.1, and about 55% fewer unnecessary blocks than Fable 5.1. In a planted sandbox-weakness test it used outside credentials in 3.1% of scenarios vs 3.3% for Opus 5.5 and 21% for Mythos 5.1.
Less comfortable system card findings, via one independent reviewer: the model suspected evaluation in up to 43% of audit transcripts; when told to sandbag and hide it, it beat an Opus 4.8 monitor about 1 in 4 times. Reward hacks succeeded in 1.0% of sampled training episodes vs 0.6% for Opus 5.5, which the card attributes to attempts succeeding more often, not more attempts. External red teams found no universal jailbreak of the cyber classifiers. For users the issue is friction: one security engineer on Hacker News said blue-team requests were still blocked. Vals saw a 0.00% refusal rate and 1.88% fallback rate on ordinary work.
Head-to-head 🥊
🥊 Only numbers found in sources
              Fable5.2 Opus5.5 Astra  Gem4C   Son5.5
AA Index      65       59      57     60      n/a
Vals Index    71.31    70.14   65.02  70.45   70.85
FrontierCode  49.1     45.5    42.8   41.1    n/a
FrontierSWE   69.9     62.3    65.5   61.2    n/a
OSWorld 2.1   89.3     87.2    79.5   81.5    n/a
HLE tools     74.2     67.7    57.2   n/a     n/a
AutomationB   51.4     42.5    41.4   53.9🏆  44.6*
AA-3D Elo     1271     1202    1168   n/a     1204
$ in/out      8/40     4/20    10/50  2/10**  2/10
* Zapier post  ** announced intro price
Cheaper models close the gap on some tests. Kimi K3.1 Pro scores 46 on Artificial Analysis vs 65, but 63.64% vs 65.15% on Vals Terminal-Bench 4.0, at $2/$10. DeepSeek V4 Pro lists at $1.32/$3.96 at peak; V4.1 Flash scores 33 on Artificial Analysis. Grok 4.7 lists at $2/$6 up to 200K tokens. I found no third-party run with Grok 4.7 and Fable 5.2 side by side, so I am not comparing their scores.
Cost analysis 💸
Token price and task price point in opposite directions.
💸 $ per Artificial Analysis index task
Fable Low     54  $3.10  ███
Fable Medium  56  $3.80  ████
Fable High    62  $9.08  █████████
Fable Xhigh   62  $14.83 ███████████████
Fable Max     65  $26.54 ███████████████████████████
Opus 5.5 max  59  $10.04
Astra max     57  $6.24
Kimi K3.1 Pro 46  $3.68
High and Xhigh score the same; High costs 61% as much. Max adds 3 points for 2.9x the cost of High. At Max, Fable 5.2 costs about twice Fable 5.1 per task despite the 20% price cut, because it wrote 275M output tokens vs 163M.
Caching is where it wins. One consultancy's worked agent turn (120K cached tokens, 2K new input, 1K output) costs $0.080 on Fable 5.2, $0.100 on Fable 5.1 and $0.190 on GPT-6 Astra, whose cache read is $1.00 per million. If your agent resends context and writes little, Fable is cheap per turn. If it thinks a lot, it is not.
The plan math confused people too. One Hacker News commenter said they needed "a fable reset to explain to me the rules of fable resets," comparing it unfavorably to AWS pricing. The short version: a reset refunds the weekly usage you spent on Fable and refills the five-hour window, but does not raise the 50% cap.
Subscribers felt it fast. One Hacker News user on the $200 plan burned two resets in under three hours, and added that it "aced the tasks." One small independent test suite cost $29.56 on Fable 5.2 vs $13.55 on Opus 5.5, with similar accuracy on short tasks.
The tier list 🏆
Relative to the current frontier, weighted toward independent results.
🏆 Fable 5.2 tier list

🟪 S  Long-horizon agentic coding
      Long-running agents / remote work
      Reasoning
      Math

🟦 A  Design, frontend and 3D
      Computer use
      Vision and charts
      Long context
      Science and engineering
      Business workflow automation

🟩 B  Writing
      Legal, tax, accounting, medical
      Safety and alignment

🟨 C  Speed at high effort
      Cost per task at Xhigh/Max
      Cyber and bio work (blocked)
🟪 S, coding: #1 on FrontierCode 2.0 and FrontierSWE v2 (vendor), #1 on Vibe Code Bench, Terminal-Bench 4.0 (tie) and ProgramBench (Vals). Loses only SWE-bench Multimodal.
🟪 S, agents: Remote Labor Index at about double every rival, WANDR 82.1%, and the 1,000-agent Lean run.
🟪 S, reasoning: #1 on Artificial Analysis, Vals and Epoch ECI, HLE 74.2%, ARC-AGI-2 93.8% verified.
🟪 S, math: FrontierMath 95% (Tiers 1-3) and 100% (Tier 4) on Epoch, best on the board.
🟦 A, design: #1 on AA-3D by 67 points and LiveBench Design, but no human-vote arena score yet and documented taste misses.
🟦 A, computer use: 89.3% partial, only 1.4 points over Opus 5.5 on strict.
🟦 A, vision: narrow Chartography lead, #1 on one detection board, 8 points behind Opus on SWE-bench Multimodal.
🟦 A, long context: 10/10 at 892K in one test, behind Opus 5.5 on full-context ProgramBench.
🟦 A, science: BenchCAD 83.5 vs 65.3 for Opus, but GPT-6 Astra leads the Vals Science Index (65.09% vs 63.74%) and Vals' Terminal-Bench-Science (62.86% vs 55.71%), reversing Anthropic's own run.
🟦 A, workflows: second to Gemini 4 Carbon on AutomationBench.
🟩 B, writing: no independent score, verbosity 72nd of 73, documented bloat.
🟩 B, domain work: #1 finance, mid-table legal and tax, one accounting regression, behind Opus on PhysicianBench.
🟩 B, safety: better alignment scores, 55% fewer false blocks, offset by high evaluation awareness and monitor evasion when instructed.
🟨 C, speed: 72nd of 73, 44.1 min per index task at max.
🟨 C, cost: 73rd of 73 at max, $26.54 per task. High alone would rate B.
🟨 C, cyber and bio: blocked by design unless you qualify for Mythos.
Who should use it 🧩
✅ Fable 5.2 at High for long autonomous coding, migrations in unfamiliar codebases, and bugs that survive several rounds on Opus.
✅ As Advisor or Orchestrator over Sonnet 5.5 or Opus 5.5 workers, so the expensive model plans and reviews while cheaper models spend most of the tokens.
✅ Multi-day agent projects with a measurable target: tests, proofs, specs.
✅ Long-context agents with heavy caching, at $0.20 per million cached tokens.
⚠️ Xhigh only where your own evals show a gain. Avoid Max as a default; it scored below Xhigh on FrontierCode and ARC-AGI-3.
❌ Stay on Opus 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5 for everyday coding, chat and short tasks. Sonnet is within half a point on Vals at a quarter of the price.
❌ Test Gemini 4 Carbon for SaaS automation and GPT-6 Astra for science analysis.
❌ Look elsewhere for tight short prose, latency-sensitive apps, and security or biology work.
What I could not verify 🔍
❓ No human-vote scores yet on LMArena, WebDev Arena, DesignArena or EQ-Bench. Writing claims are qualitative.
❓ SWE-bench Pro 93.0%, Terminal-Bench 4.0 67.6%, PhysicianBench and full-context ProgramBench come from secondary write-ups quoting the 264-page system card, which I could not open directly.
❓ No current SWE-bench Verified score (Vals archived it as saturated) and no METR time-horizon figure.
❓ No outside replication of RoboDojo, AutomationBench, the cyber rows, the Fermat run or the hardware demo, and no third-party check on "30% faster" or "55% fewer blocks."
❓ One X user posted a $642.42 run at an "Ultra" effort. Anthropic's docs list Low through Max only.
❓ One aggregator lists 46 tok/s via OpenRouter vs Artificial Analysis' 103. I could not reconcile them.
❓ A Hacker News thread claimed Opus 5.5 was degraded before launch. Two commenters re-ran their own evals and found no regression. I found nothing conclusive.

Evaluating AI agents involves moving beyond simple metrics toward rigorous, multi-dimensional assessment. In his talk, Alex Ratner outlines that because AI capabilities now outpace traditional measurement, we must adopt more sophisticated, realistic testing environments .

Ratner identifies three key axes to effectively benchmark modern AI agents:

Environment Complexity: Moving from isolated, self-contained tasks (like basic coding exams) to messy, real-world contexts. This requires agents to navigate tools, interfaces (like OSWorld 2.0), and messy repositories 

Autonomy Horizon: Measuring an agent’s performance on long-term, dynamic tasks. This assesses not just the ability to complete a single step, but to adapt when goals shift, demonstrating capabilities like continual learning.

Nuanced Verifiability: Shifting away from binary unit tests (which only check if an answer is "correct") toward evaluating qualitative output. This includes judging code quality, architectural decision-making, and stylistic "taste," such as in Senior SWE-bench.

To prevent "benchmaxxing" (overfitting to public leaderboards), Ratner emphasizes that organizations should prioritize continuous benchmarks that evolve like open-source projects, ensuring they remain robust and resistant to being gamed.

We're gradually shifting our focus beyond SWE in our work on RL environments and agent training/inference, while wrapping up our planned SWE releases.

Today we released LongTail-SWE (not our last SWE release), a benchmark covering 13 languages that have been largely overlooked in coding-agent evaluations: Clojure, Dart, Elixir, Erlang, F#, Haskell, Julia, Kotlin, Lua, OCaml, R, Scala, and Swift.

A couple of observations from building environments.

First, constructing hard, high-quality RL environments is getting increasingly difficult. As models improve, we need to keep raising task difficulty. But harder tasks also increase the risk of broken verification, undetected reward hacking, or accidentally introducing unsolvable problems that you think to be just challenging.

This creates a continuous feedback loop: we need better tools for trajectory monitoring and environment quality control, which in turn reveal more issues to address.

LongTail-SWE is our attempt to build challenging environments without compromising their quality. We evaluate problem statements and fail-to-pass tests through multiple rounds of LLM judges, which we calibrated separately for this purpose. Other models then use their feedback to fix tests and supplement task information.

Second, coding tasks with a reasonable scope are getting close to saturation for frontier models. GPT-6 Astra (xhigh) with context compaction can solve most of them, especially SWE-bench-like tasks.

So what if your local MoE model needed less memory and still handled coding tasks about as well? 

So Amazon researchers removed 50% of the experts from Qwen3.5-35B-A3B using HOPE.

Their reported SWE-Bench Pro scores...
🟢 Original model → 41.8
🟢 HOPE, 50% of experts removed → 42.3
🔴 REAP, 50% removed → 36.2

HOPE stands for Higher-Order Pruning of Experts.
Instead of scoring each expert independently, it also considers how pairs of experts work together when deciding which ones to remove.

So for Local AI, this is the appeal
💾 Smaller checkpoints
🧠 Lower model-weight memory requirements
📚 Potentially more room for context
🔧 No retraining required
⚙️ Can be combined with quantization

HOPE code is Apache 2.0.

The process is to collect statistics using calibration prompts, select experts to remove, then export a smaller Hugging Face checkpoint.

Here are the limits...
Removing half the experts doesn’t halve every component of the model. These are researcher-reported results, and preserving one benchmark score doesn’t guarantee unchanged performance everywhere.

Picking an AI agent using benchmarks not even used by OpenAI.

In Feburary, OpenAI stopped publishing results on SWE-bench Verified (where for some tasks, models from 3 labs, including GPT-5.2, can replicate the reference fix from the task ID or short hint). They recommended using SWE-Bench Pro but retracted that recommendation on July 8 (as around 30% of tasks had errors). Within less than 5 months, someone had selected an agent for their team.

HumanEval is even worse. It consists of 164 tasks at an easy interview question level (as stated by the authors). It has been heavily boasted about in announcements of coding models over the past few years. NVIDIA ran testing using 10 models and found a correlation of around -0.4. That means there is an inverse correlation. The higher the HumanEval score, the worse the agent performed on average after fine-tuning in this sample.

The new benchmark is from NVIDIA (Paper: Before They Can Solve by 22 authors). They use a log of a strong agent solving a real task and identify the critical step. This is the first edit that makes the projects tests pass. They run testing on the base model. One of the 3 checks is how obvious this step is to the model. When ranked by this metric, the order of the 10 models matched the final rankings with a correlation of ~0.96.

The approach is a nice one, and I like it. However, it relies heavily on the SWE-bench Verified test which was abandoned by OpenAI. While they have validated using other benchmarks, there are only 10 models and no confidence intervals. They state the numbers are descriptive. They require logs of an agent stronger than the one you're selecting. This means it isn't very useful for the top ones. There are no values for cost (which is the whole point). One of the logs for their own model Nemotron-3-Ultra had an inflated score.

The market for agents is similar. Only around 130 out of thousands of vendors stating that they have an agentic product actually do (Gartner estimate). Over 40% of agent projects will be abandoned by the end of 2027 (Gartner forecast). Anthropic have some interesting guidance. Claude Opus 4.5 scored 42% on CORE-Bench. However, they found issues in the test itself. The check marked their answer down as it was expecting 96.124991 but they had answered with 96.12. After fixing the issues and changing the harness, it scored 95%.

If I were a company looking to select an agent, I would only look at the leaderboards for initial filtering. I would gather 20-50 private tasks (Anthropic recommend you start with this amount) from my own tracker. These should have an accepted solution and tests. Then I would provide the candidate with the history up to when the key decision was made.

Next time someone in the chat asks what agent to get, this link will be useful. Bookmark and follow me to continue reading these types of breakdowns.

Fable 5.2 on ARC-AGI-3: context and runtime shape the score

Anthropic has released Claude Fable 5.2. ARC Prize’s independent evaluation of an earlier checkpoint shows how much the surrounding setup matters: at high reasoning effort, it scored 79.3% with the Standard harness and 97.7% with the Provider Adapter.

ARC-AGI-3 measures how efficiently models learn and act in unfamiliar interactive games, relative to human performance. The two harnesses use the same games, actions, limits and scoring, while handling conversation context differently.

The Standard harness carries a provider-neutral text history and model-selected visible notes. The Provider Adapter preserves native reasoning state and uses history compaction. ARC Prize reports their scores separately. The attached ARC Prize chart shows both configurations; the comparison includes context management as part of the tested system.

Runtime also changes the picture. In the Standard harness, the evaluated checkpoint scored 81.2% at xhigh and 65.7% at max. At max, 28 of 55 semi-private games reached the 12-hour runtime limit, capping progress. That result reflects the available time budget as well as the effort setting. An uncapped max score remains unmeasured in this report.

There is a version detail to carry forward: ARC Prize says the shipping model uses different tuning at medium and xhigh from the checkpoint it evaluated. Low, high and max are unchanged. The 81.2% xhigh result belongs to that earlier checkpoint.

For a deployment trial, record the model version, context policy, reasoning effort and deadline alongside completion and cost. Those settings make a benchmark result useful when choosing how to run a long task.

• Grouping documents for retrieval

If you want to build a gigafactory for bipedal robots or spin up a 100,000-GPU cluster, you do not just plug into the local power grid. You need high-capacity step-down transformers to drop 345kV transmission voltage down to usable industrial levels.

Lead times for large power transformers in the United States currently sit between 3 and 4 years.

First, grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES). High-efficiency transformer cores require specialized magnetic steel with specific crystal orientations to minimize eddy current losses. Only a handful of mills on Earth can manufacture it at scale, and global supply is severely backlogged.

Second, skilled manual labor. Winding high-voltage copper and aluminum coils for 100MVA transformers is not fully automated. It requires experienced coil winders, and the workforce has been shrinking for two decades.

Third, regulatory queue bottlenecks. Interconnection queues with regional transmission operators like PJM and ERCOT now stretch past 2029 for major industrial loads.

This is why companies like Tesla and hyperscalers are quietly stockpiling utility transformers on open gravel lots and buying up gas turbine rental fleets.

They know compute hardware is easy to buy. Getting 100 megawatts of physical power delivered to your building is the actual competitive moat.

Without transformers, your supercomputer is just a very expensive warehouse of silicon bricks.

财联社C50风向指数调查：10月新增信贷或同比少增，社融有望同比多增

财联社11月9日讯（记者夏淑媛） 新一期财联社“C50风向指数”结果显示，10月金融数据或将呈现社融改善、信贷收缩的态势。信贷方面，10月新增人民币贷款或再现负值，市场机构预测中值为-1500亿元；同期新增社融预测中值为1.5万亿元，或实现同比多增6800亿元。货币增速来看，10月末M1、M2同比增速或双双小幅回落。

物价方面，国家统计局今日公布数据显示，10月CPI同比上涨0.7%，PPI同比上涨5.7%刷新年内新高。而此前市场机构对10月CPI同比增速的预测中值为0.8%，对PPI的预测中值为5.3%，实际数据与预测值整体契合。

“C50风向指数调查”是由财联社发起，由市场中的各类研究机构参与完成，结果能够较为全面地反映市场机构对于宏观经济走势、货币政策感受以及金融数据的预期。共有近20家机构参与本期调查。

10月新增人民币贷款或同比少增，市场预测中值为-1500亿元

9月新增人民币贷款录得1.08万亿元，虽同比少增2100亿元，但较8月的600亿元大幅回升，略超市场预期。

本期调查显示，10月新增人民币贷款或再现负值，难改同比少增格局。市场机构预测中值为-1500亿元，较去年同期的2200亿元少增3700亿元，预测区间在-2000亿元至3000亿元。

市场人士指出，10月是季末集中冲量后的传统信贷“小月”，银行投放节奏通常随之放缓，主要受以下两方面因素影响：

一方面，居民端融资需求整体偏弱，新增贷款或出现负值。

从消费端看，财通证券研究所固收首席隋修平表示，10月下旬地铁出行强于季节性，但乘用车零售、电影票房偏弱，消费修复仍有分化，预计居民短贷环比多减、同比少减。

从房贷端看，高频数据显示，10月1日-29日，30大中城市商品房成交面积约543.7万平方米，较去年同期下降16.1%。隋修平认为，虽有一线城市住房成交形成一定支撑，但重点城市新房成交总体仍不及去年同期，局部改善对按揭需求全面修复的带动效果尚需观测，预计居民中长期贷款环比转负、同比多减。

另一方面，企业端融资缺乏扩张基础，信贷同比或多减。

隋修平指出，受10月制造业指数降至49.8%及季初回落影响，企业经营周转需求偏弱，预计企业短贷环比转负、同比少减；同时，建筑业指数降至48.0%且基建实物工作量传导不畅，预计中长贷同比少增。整体来看，短贷的同比少减难以抵消中长贷的回落，企业融资仍缺乏持续扩张的基础。

东方金诚宏观首席王青在接受财联社记者采访时表示：“10月新型政策性金融工具投放完毕，预计对企业中长期贷款有一定拉动作用，但难以抵消新增居民贷款为负的影响。”他进一步指出，当前票据利率处于低位且月末未见上冲，既反映信贷需求不强，也预示10月票据冲量现象仍会比较明显。

浙商证券经济学家李超表示：“10月半年期国股银票转贴现利率持续维持在0.5%左右的低位，与10月30日半年期国有大行同业存单利率的利差维持在-90BP左右，这反映出银行票据配置需求较强，而一般贷款需求依然偏弱。”

10月新增社融预测中值1.5万亿元，政策发力有望带动增速回升至7.3%

9月，新增社融规模录得3.55万亿元，同比多增200亿元，较8月同比少增9000亿元的表现明显好转。

本期调查显示，超七成机构预计政策发力有望带动社融存量增速回升至7.3%。市场机构对10月新增社融规模的预测中值为1.5万亿元，较去年同期多增6800亿元，预测区间在1万亿元至1.6万亿元。

王青表示，在投向实体经济的贷款同比多减的背景下，10月新增社融主要由政府债券融资支撑。

具体来看，四季度政府债券融资规模预计较上年同期高出1.5万亿元；单看10月，政府债券融资达1.1万亿元，同比多增约6000亿元；企业债券融资约2900亿元，同比多增近400亿元。

此外，随着10月新型政策性金融工具投放完毕，预计10月单月投放规模或在7000亿元左右，可能带动社融委托贷款同比多增。

货币增速方面，10月末M1及M2同比增速或均小幅回落。

针对M1走势，浙商证券宏观首席林成炜表示：“10月虽然8000亿元新型政策性金融工具已经完成全部投放，但资金补充项目资本金后，还需要经过项目资金拨付及实际支付才能转化为企业交易性存款，对当月M1的直接拉动有限。”其预计10月M1同比增长3.0%，M1与M2剪刀差维持在-4个百分点左右，实体经济资金活化程度仍有待改善。

M2来看，王青分析指出：“一方面，当月新增人民币贷款偏弱，会拖累存款派生；另一方面，四季度稳增长政策发力，有可能带动财政支出提速，若财政存款出现同比少增，则会对M2增速有一定推升作用。”

值得注意的是，近期贸易顺差规模高位上行，叠加人民币持续升值，企业净结汇顺差显著扩大。“这意味着10月还会有较大规模的不计入M2的企业外币资产，转化为纳入M2统计的企业存款，也会阶段性对M2增速形成支撑。”王青表示。

10月CPI同比小幅回落至0.7%，PPI同比升至5.7%刷新年内新高

10月CPI同比上涨0.7%，环比涨幅回落0.2个百分点。此前市场机构预测中值为0.8%，预测区间为0.7%-1.0%。

“10月CPI同比涨幅收窄，主要原因是蔬菜价格大幅下跌，带动食品价格同比降幅显著扩大，充分抵消了当月国际油价上涨推动国内汽油价格上调带来的影响。”王青表示。

兴业银行首席经济学家鲁政委分析指出，受长假需求退坡影响，10月食品价格多数回落。其中猪肉、鸡蛋、蔬菜价格环比分别下跌3.6%、12.6%和8.5%，对食品CPI形成明显拖累。

能源方面，10月国内成品油调价呈现“一搁浅一上调”，交通工具用能源对CPI拉动有限；同时，上海金交所黄金价格环比跌幅扩大至5.7%，拖累其他用品和服务价格。综合食品、能源及黄金价格的表现，叠加翘尾因素，10月CPI同比有所回落。

PPI方面，10月PPI同比上涨5.7%，创2022年7月以来新高，且略超市场预期。 此前，市场普遍预计10月PPI同比将再度刷新年内高点，机构预测中值为5.3%，预测区间为5.1%至5.6%。实际值已突破预测区间上限。

王青表示，10月PPI环比涨幅回落，主要源于当月国际原油、有色金属以及国内煤炭等大宗商品价格在前期较快上涨、绝对价格水平已偏高的背景下，环比上行幅度明显放缓。

“不过，在环比延续上涨带动下，10月PPI同比涨幅进一步扩大。往后看，11月PPI环比可能转跌，同比涨幅将有所回落，但年底前仍将处于4.0%以上的较快增长区间。”王青预计。

结论：国内偏多，今晚美国CPI是关键变量。
托底资金已经在真实买入，油价回落对成长股有利；海外市场已完全定价美联储12月加息，CPI若偏热，会先压美股AI链，再传导到A股光模块和算力龙头。今晚不因政策消息追高。

1/ 中国10月CPI/PPI：CPI同比+0.7%，核心+0.8%，均回落0.2个百分点；PPI同比+5.7%，扩大0.7个百分点，主要靠能源（煤炭+36.6%、油气开采+35.0%），AI也带动存储设备、电脑涨价。内需仍弱，涨价来自上游和AI。
2/ 10月出口：按人民币计同比+28.7%，前10个月货物贸易+20%，财新称主要由AI相关贸易拉动。
3/ 托底政策落地：央行11-03开展第三批互换便利，中信、中金、国信、中泰、中信建投等券商已完成首批买股；回购增持再贷款转为长期安排、利率降到1%；证监会表示研究优化融资保证金比例，"适度释放融资空间"。

Twice the Fed Tried to Shrink Its Balance Sheet, and Twice the Plumbing Pushed Back. Now Warsh Wants a Third Go.

The Federal Reserve's balance sheet peaked at nearly $9 trillion in 2022, after successive rounds of crisis-era bond buying that began in 2008 and ballooned during the pandemic. Between June 2022 and December 2025, quantitative tightening, or QT, cut total assets by roughly $2.4 trillion, to about $6.5 trillion. That sounds like a large retreat until you set it against the starting line: the balance sheet at the end of 2025 was still more than 50% above its pre-COVID size and over seven times its size before the financial crisis. The mechanism itself is almost boringly simple. When a Treasury bond the Fed owns matures, the Treasury pays the Fed back, and the Fed, instead of using that money to buy a new bond, lets it vanish, which shrinks both its holdings and the stock of money it created. There's a second, more aggressive version, outright selling, which the Bank of England has used and the Fed has not. When the Fed first launched QT in 2017, officials famously described it as being like "watching paint dry": interest rates would do the heavy lifting, and balance sheet runoff would hum along quietly in the background. A Goldman Sachs explainer puts the logic of the two tools in a sentence worth remembering: rate hikes change the price of short-term money directly, while QT works through quantities, reducing reserves and bond holdings, and so reaches longer-term yields and financial conditions by a slower and less visible route. That quiet-background plan survived contact with reality for a couple of years each time. Then, in September 2019 and again in the fall of 2025, the Fed discovered that its paint was in fact a plumbing system, and the Fed has now stopped QT, restarted modest purchases, and handed the whole problem to a new chair who has said, repeatedly, that the balance sheet should shrink a lot more.

Where the money actually comes out of

The part almost nobody explains clearly is the liability side of the ledger, because that's where QT bites. A central bank's balance sheet has to balance. If the Fed's assets shrink by a trillion dollars, something on the other side has to shrink by a trillion dollars too, and there are really only two candidates. One is the overnight reverse repo facility, where money market funds park spare cash with the Fed overnight. The other is reserves, the deposits commercial banks hold at the Fed, which they use to settle payments with each other and which also serve as their ultimate safety cushion. In the first stretch of QT, the drain came mostly out of the reverse repo facility, which had swollen to enormous size, and banks barely noticed. Once that pool ran dry, every further dollar of runoff came straight out of bank reserves. Reserves had hit an all-time high of more than $4.2 trillion in December 2021. By 2025 they were near $3 trillion, about 12% of bank assets, according to Barclays, and a third force was draining them at the same time: the Treasury, which has to issue a great deal of debt to fund large deficits and park the proceeds in its own account at the Fed, pulls cash out of the banking system whenever it rebuilds that account. One analysis counted over $1.5 trillion of net new Treasury issuance in fiscal 2025 alone. The Fed was shrinking reserves from one side while the government was soaking them up from the other, and neither agency was fully coordinating with the other. Central bankers describe the target as "ample" reserves, meaning enough that banks never have to scramble for cash. The uncomfortable truth, which the Fed freely admits, is that nobody knows in advance where ample ends and scarce begins. As Russell Investments puts it, the Fed doesn't and can't know the exact tipping point, so it reads market signals for signs it's getting close. In practice that means the Fed finds the limit by hitting it.

▍1. Anthropic Releases Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 for 50+ Step Long-Horizon Agentic Engineering
Anthropic announced the enterprise rollout of Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, two specialized foundation models engineered specifically for multi-hour, long-horizon software engineering. Rather than optimizing purely for single-turn coding benchmarks, Anthropic trained these architectures on extended trajectories exceeding fifty continuous tool invocations, directly tackling the cognitive drift that derails autonomous coding agents during multi-repository refactoring.
The architectural advancement lies in hierarchical action-state checkpointing paired with trajectory reinforcement learning. When an agent executes complex codebase migrations, standard autoregressive models suffer from compounding error rates as failed attempts accumulate in the active context window. Fable 5.2 introduces native rollback semantics directly into its decoding loop, enabling the model to prune dead-end exploratory paths and branch into alternative architectural implementations without human intervention.
However, long-horizon autonomy introduces significant operational cost and execution latency trade-offs. Running fifty-step autonomous loops consumes massive token budgets, often costing tens of dollars per pull request while saturating dedicated inference capacity. Engineering organizations integrating Mythos and Fable into CI/CD pipelines must enforce strict unit test gating and deterministic timeout circuits to prevent autonomous agents from spiraling into runaway debugging loops on ambiguous specifications.

▍2. Stanford Introduces Next-Concept Modeling to Replace Token Autoregression with Latent Concept Skeletons
AI researchers at Stanford University published a paradigm-shifting research paper introducing Next-Concept Modeling (NCM), an architectural framework designed to dismantle traditional token-by-token autoregression. Instead of predicting individual subword tokens sequentially, NCM generates high-level semantic concept vectors in a continuous latent space before decoding them in parallel into final syntactic code or structured natural language.
The technique directly targets the severe computational bottlenecks and structural myopia inherent in standard autoregressive transformers. By shifting the primary planning mechanism to an abstract concept level, the model decouples macro-architectural reasoning from surface-level syntax generation. Empirical benchmarks demonstrate a fourfold acceleration in inference decoding speeds alongside dramatic reductions in logical inconsistencies across complex multi-file software engineering tasks.
Nevertheless, non-autoregressive latent decoding introduces tricky alignment and structural hallucination risks for enterprise production systems. When an abstract concept vector fails to ground properly during parallel token expansion, the resulting output can contain mathematically invalid syntax or non-existent library dependencies that look superficially plausible. Systems architects evaluating latent planning models must incorporate deterministic abstract syntax tree parsers and language compilers directly into generation pipelines to validate code before execution.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
▍3. llama-modchip Runs 284B DeepSeek Model on 64GB RAM Pure-CPU at 14 tok/s via Fractal-64 Quantization
An open-source systems project titled llama-modchip went viral across the developer community, demonstrating that a massive 284-billion-parameter DeepSeek model can run on commodity consumer CPUs with just 64GB of RAM. Achieving sustained inference throughput between 9.1 and 14.7 tokens per second on modern AMD Zen 5 and Apple Silicon architectures, the project completely eliminates the requirement for enterprise GPU clusters for local inference.
The breakthrough relies on extreme 1.71-bit "Fractal-64" micro-quantization paired with AVX-512 register tiling and a speculative tree search engine inspired by the Stockfish chess engine. By compressing the model footprint down to 57GB, the runtime streams active weights directly through CPU caches without saturating system memory bandwidth. The architecture dynamically predicts speculative token sequences, evaluating multiple candidate branches simultaneously to mask memory bus latency.
While this unlocks frontier-scale model experimentation on developer workstations, extreme sub-2-bit quantization extracts a measurable precision tax. Symbolic mathematics, precise regex generation, and multi-step cryptographic proofs exhibit noticeable degradation compared to full-precision FP16 weights. Platform engineers must treat hyper-quantized CPU models as rapid local drafting engines, routing mission-critical verification steps to higher-precision cloud models.

▍4. ChatGPT Desktop Silently Forwards Host SSH Agent Sockets, Exposing Private Keys to Remote Hosts
Security researchers disclosed a severe vulnerability in OpenAI's official ChatGPT desktop application, revealing that the client silently forwards the host machine's active SSH Agent Unix socket during remote execution sessions. Without displaying explicit confirmation dialogs or notifying the developer, the desktop tool exposes local developer authentication keys to any remote container or server connected to the workflow.
The issue stems from a classic developer-convenience misconfiguration in underlying terminal forwarding libraries. In an effort to streamline remote Git commits and cloud server deployments, the client defaults to transparent agent forwarding rather than enforcing isolated session authentication. Consequently, a compromised remote development server or malicious third-party repository script can access the forwarded socket, hijacking developer credentials to authenticate against internal corporate infrastructure.
This flaw highlights the urgent necessity of isolating desktop AI tools from host operating system credentials. Treating AI desktop assistants as privileged administrative utilities creates massive lateral attack surfaces across enterprise networks. DevSecOps leads must enforce strict endpoint policies that disable SSH Agent forwarding by default, mandating containerized sandbox runtimes and ephemeral, password-protected hardware security keys for all developer workstations.

Cloud cybersecurity firm Apiiro published an alarming security audit revealing that Claude Code has leaked over 2,500 sensitive credentials across more than 1,100 public GitHub repositories. The leaks occur when developers select the convenient "Allow and don't ask again" prompt in the CLI, which writes raw execution commands containing plaintext API tokens and cloud secrets directly into `.claude/settings.local.json`.
The vulnerability originates from a critical omission in default project initialization templates. Platform teams deploying autonomous coding assistants must deploy automated pre-commit secret scanners across developer machines and enforce centralized secret managers to inject credentials at runtime rather than storing them in local dotfiles.

Five Hundred Stocks, Ten Real Bets: Does Everyone Owning the Same Thing Create a New Kind of Systemic Risk?

Michael Burry, the investor made famous by The Big Short, warned in 2019 that passive investing was inflating a bubble. The logic was easy to follow: if a huge share of the world's savings automatically buys the same list of companies in the same proportions, then everyone is on one side of one trade, and a crowd that size can't all leave through the same door at once. It's an appealing story, and it's half right, which is why it's useful to pull it apart. There are two different claims hiding inside it. One is about the individual saver, whose portfolio may be far more concentrated than it looks. The other is about the financial system, whose stability could depend on how index funds behave when everyone panics at once. The evidence for the first claim is strong and getting stronger. The evidence for the second is thinner, more technical, and in places points the opposite way. Four Federal Reserve researchers, Kenechukwu Anadu, Patrick McCabe, Mathias Kruttli, Emilio Osambela and Chae Hee Shin, took the second question seriously in a paper published in the Financial Analysts Journal, examining four channels: redemption risk, volatility, concentration among asset managers, and valuations and correlations. Their conclusion was that the shift to passive had reduced some risks and increased others, with no red lights flashing. The UK's Financial Conduct Authority reached a similar verdict on ETFs around the same time. That doesn't settle anything for 2026, when passive money is far larger and the largest companies carry far more weight, but it explains why the honest answer to this question has to be sorted channel by channel instead of delivered as a verdict.

The channel where passive is actually the safer design

Start with the one most people get backwards. The classic financial crisis mechanism is a run: investors want their money back, the fund must sell assets to pay them, selling pushes prices down, and falling prices frighten more investors into redeeming. Mutual funds are vulnerable to this because they promise daily cash redemptions regardless of how liquid their holdings are, and investors tend to redeem when performance is poor. The Fed researchers argue that moving assets from active mutual funds into passive ETFs generally reduces this risk, for two reasons. Most ETF redemptions are settled in kind, meaning the ETF hands over a basket of the underlying securities in exchange for its own shares, so the fund doesn't have to sell into a falling market to raise cash. And a passive fund can't meaningfully underperform its benchmark, which removes one of the main triggers for investors to flee a fund in the first place. The caveat they attach is worth keeping in mind: the stability benefit shrinks if future ETF growth is dominated by products that redeem in cash. The stress episodes so far are a mixed record.

On August 24, 2015, the Dow fell more than 1,000 points within the first minutes of trading, and some equity ETFs dropped far more than the stocks inside them, which alarmed a lot of investors who had placed stop-loss orders. The fund industry's own account, published by the Investment Company Institute, blames structural flaws in the equity market that temporarily broke the arbitrage mechanism linking ETF prices to their holdings, and the dislocation mostly worked itself out by the close. March 2020 was harder to explain away. According to the Bank of England, some of the largest investment-grade and high-yield corporate bond ETFs traded at discounts to their net asset value of more than 5%, after having been no larger than 0.1% earlier in the year, and the Vanguard Total Bond Market ETF hit a 6.2% discount. The BIS read the episode as ETFs providing price discovery while the underlying bond market had seized up and the quoted values were stale.
